clue.text: There are four of these in the Square displaying very devious motive

definitions.text: There are four of these in the Square

parts.note: right is an old intensifier meaning very, as in 'a right good time' or 'Right Honourable'
an angle is a hidden or self-serving motive, as in 'what's his angle?'

explanation.surface: A puzzle about some shady scheme cooked up in a town square.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Square' looks like Albert Square from EastEnders, in keeping with the Cockney theme, but it is any geometric square, whose four corners are each ninety degrees.
explanation.definitionFit: Every corner of a square is a ninety-degree corner, so a square has four of them.

clue.text: Bear up over the French state's nonsense

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece placed over another comes before it
in a down clue, up means the word is read from the bottom, so backwards

parts.note: Pooh is the famous bear of A. A. Milne's stories
la is the French feminine word for the

explanation.surface: Someone dismisses a French state's claims as rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'state's' is a link meaning 'is', joining the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Hoopla is fuss or ballyhoo, a synonym for empty commotion and nonsense.

clue.text: Positive answer restrains student's cry of alarm

indicators.note: to restrain is to hold in, so one piece is held inside the other

parts.note: yep is an informal yes
L is the learner driver's plate, standing for a student

explanation.surface: A student cries out after hearing yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A yelp is a short sharp shriek, the kind given in sudden pain or fright.

clue.text: Den climbs under partner, having physical relationship

indicators.note: in a down entry, a piece under another follows it

parts.note: a mate is a partner or spouse

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means the word goes upwards, read backwards

parts.note: a lair is a wild animal's den

explanation.surface: Someone moves into a lover's den and the relationship turns physical.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' and 'relationship' are padding for the surface; the definition is 'physical'.
explanation.definitionFit: Material things are corporeal, made of matter rather than spirit.

clue.text: Last of me mother's cheese

indicators.note: taking the last of a word means its final letter only

parts.note: a dam is a mother, especially of an animal

explanation.surface: A child claims the final bit of mum's cheese.
explanation.definitionFit: Edam is a mild Dutch cheese with a red wax rind.

clue.text: Spiky cockney's socks put on to dry

indicators.note: one piece is added on to the end of the other

parts.note: to spin is to dry washing in a spin-dryer

indicators.note: a Cockney speaker drops the H at the start of a word

parts.note: hose are stockings or socks

explanation.surface: A Londoner's spiky socks are hung out to dry.
explanation.walkthrough: In the surface 'dry' is what socks are put out to do; here it is the spin cycle, and 'cockney's' is the H-dropping habit applied to the socks.
explanation.definitionFit: Spinose is the botanical word for covered in spines, so prickly.

clue.text: See 22
Tried out 'at oddly rejected after returning for close inspection

indicators.note: thrown back on the way home, so the picked letters are turned round
oddly means the letters in odd positions are kept, first, third, fifth and so on

explanation.surface: A Cockney auditioning for a hat-shop job is turned down and sent home.
explanation.walkthrough: The odd letters of 'Tried out 'at' give TIDUA, and 'rejected after returning' turns them round.
explanation.definitionFit: An audit is a formal, detailed examination of accounts.

clue.text: Country is enthralled by first class head having ascended

indicators.note: held captive by, so one piece sits inside the other
in a down clue, going up means the pieces read backwards

parts.note: A1 means first class, written AI with I for one
nut is slang for head

explanation.surface: A top-ranking leader rises and is held in thrall.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 for first class is written with the letter I for the figure one; 'having ascended' turns both pieces upwards, and 'enthralled by' holds IS inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Tunisia is a North African nation on the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Traffic illegally parking acceptable on the edges of Shoreditch

parts.note: P is the parking sign
U means socially acceptable, from 'U and non-U' upper-class usage

indicators.note: the edges of a word are its first and last letters

explanation.surface: Illegal trading round the parking spots of Shoreditch, a district of East London.
explanation.definitionFit: To push drugs is slang for dealing them illegally.

clue.text: Dot's load of dosh is sweet

parts.note: to pepper is to dot or sprinkle all over
a mint is a huge sum of money

explanation.surface: A woman called Dot has piles of cash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dot' reads as a Cockney name (Dot Cotton of EastEnders) but is a verb. The 's is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A peppermint is a mint-flavoured boiled confection.

clue.text: 'As the pan boiling for game bird

indicators.note: boiling stirs things about, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Cockney cook says the pan is boiling for the bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A pheasant is a long-tailed bird shot for sport and eaten.

clue.text: Tax position dogs that man in Deptford

indicators.note: to dog is to follow, so one piece comes after the other
Deptford is in South East London, where a Cockney accent drops the H

parts.note: him refers to that man
a post is a job or position

explanation.surface: A position follows a man round Deptford, demanding tax.
explanation.walkthrough: Deptford is in South East London, where H-dropping Cockney speech is assumed; 'dogs' means follows, so the job comes after the man.
explanation.definitionFit: An impost is a levy or duty.

clue.text: Rabbiting, like Mike Reid, perhaps, about Natalie's first modelling

indicators.note: a word placed about another goes round it

parts.note: pattering is chattering, as the comedian Mike Reid did; rabbit and pork is rhyming slang for talk

indicators.note: the first letter of the word only

explanation.surface: An actor from EastEnders chats away about a girl called Natalie.
explanation.walkthrough: Mike Reid was a Cockney comic who played Frank Butcher in EastEnders.
explanation.definitionFit: Patterning is shaping by a model or making decorative designs, as modelling does.

clue.text: With 18, the way amphibians coupled

annotationWithheld.why: With 18, the way amphibians coupled (4): the answer is the linked phrase FROG AND TOAD (rhyming slang for road), but the puzzle file does not group 15-across with 18-across, so no wordplay for the lone light is possible

clue.text: Bird I'm missing during stretch for repeat lesson

indicators.note: one piece sits inside the period of the other

parts.note: to reach is to stretch out

indicators.note: missing means those letters are taken away

parts.note: bird is slang for a prison sentence, time inside, from bird lime, rhyming slang for time
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prison term is spent learning the same lesson again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bird' is prison time from rhyming slang (bird lime = time), and 'stretch' is also prison slang, so the surface reads as a jail term; 'I'm missing' strips IM, and 'during' puts the rest inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To reteach is to give the same instruction once more.

clue.text: See 12

annotationWithheld.why: See 12: second half of the linked phrase TWIST AND TWIRL, which the puzzle file does not group with 12-down

clue.text: Rarely attractive careless faults including the missing aitch

indicators.note: carelessly put together, so the letters are jumbled
dropped, as a Cockney drops the letter

parts.note: aitch is the spelt-out name of H

explanation.surface: Careless faults, like dropping an aitch, are rarely attractive.
explanation.walkthrough: THE without H gives TE, which joins FAULTS in the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Tasteful means showing good, refined judgment, an uncommonly pleasing quality.

clue.text: See 15

annotationWithheld.why: See 15: second half of the linked phrase FROG AND TOAD, which the puzzle file does not group with 15-across

clue.text: Get anxious suspect gutted about disturbed rest

indicators.note: one piece is placed round another
gutting takes out the insides, leaving only the outside letters

parts.note: to suss is slang for suspect or work out

indicators.note: disturbed letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A suspect becomes jittery after a broken night.
explanation.walkthrough: Suss is British slang for suspect; 'gutted' empties it to its outer letters, and 'about' wraps them round 'rest' after 'disturbed' jumbles it.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress is informal for to worry or fret.

clue.text: Cross barrow boys possibly'd missed out, substituted by very early starter

indicators.note: the letter D is left out and something else takes its place

parts.note: barrow boys are street traders who sell from carts

indicators.note: the starter is the first letter only

explanation.surface: Street traders in a market try to get across.
explanation.walkthrough: Replacing D in TRADERS with V gives TRAVERS, then E from 'early'.
explanation.definitionFit: To traverse is to go across or through.

clue.text: Arguin' about a weapon

indicators.note: about signals moving the letters around

explanation.surface: A Cockney argues over a gun.
explanation.definitionFit: An airgun fires pellets using compressed air.

clue.text: Partner follows warm and friendly kisser

indicators.note: one piece comes after the other

parts.note: a sunny person is cheerful and genial
in bridge, South is North's partner

explanation.surface: A partner follows a warm, friendly kisser.
explanation.walkthrough: SUNNY SOUTH is Cockney rhyming slang for mouth; kisser is slang for mouth.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhyming slang: a phrase rhyming with mouth stands for it, and kisser is slang for the mouth.

clue.text: Having taken out half a London street Carter may provide for him

definitions.text: Having taken out half a London street Carter may provide for him

indicators.note: taking away half of a two-part name leaves the other part

parts.note: Pall Mall is a famous street in London's West End
a carter carries goods, so is a bearer

explanation.surface: A gangster named Carter supplies a coffin carrier for his victims.
explanation.walkthrough: Carter evokes the hit man of the film Get Carter, who provides corpses: hence the whole clue defines one who carries coffins.
explanation.definitionFit: A bearer carries a coffin at a funeral, someone a killer indirectly supplies work for.

clue.text: Possibly Deighton's mince pie ingredient

definitions.meaning: Len Deighton is the spy novelist, so the possessive belongs to Len
mince pies is rhyming slang for eyes, and the clear focusing part of an eye is in each

explanation.definitionFit: An eye contains a transparent focusing body; Len Deighton's first name plus 's gives the same letters.

clue.text: Prince raised a glass

indicators.note: in a down clue, raised means read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: a jar is a glass of beer

explanation.surface: Someone raises a glass to a prince.
explanation.definitionFit: A raja is an Indian prince or king.

clue.text: Negative response by no good nitwit

parts.note: no is a negative answer

explanation.surface: A fool answers no, and is no good.
explanation.definitionFit: Nong is Australian slang for a fool.

clue.text: 'E's a religious follower takin' part in churchin', duck

indicators.note: taking part in means a piece of the words is used

explanation.surface: A Cockney churchgoer joins the church service, love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'E's is a link meaning he is; duck is a Cockney term of endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: A Hindu is an adherent of Hinduism.

clue.text: Trip young man carrying vase

indicators.note: carrying means holding the other piece inside

parts.note: Joey is a lad's name, used for a young fellow
an urn is a vase

explanation.surface: A young man carries a vase on a trip.
explanation.definitionFit: A journey is a trip from one place to another.
